usage: time adverbial: 과거에는 ~ used to contrast with now
natural collocation; 돌아보다 = to reflect on
pairs with 먼/가까운 to describe how far back
grammar term: the past-tense form of a verb
examples: 과거에는 이 동네가 다 논밭이었어요.
In the past, this whole neighborhood was rice fields.
과거에(는) sets up a contrast with the present
이제 과거는 잊고 앞으로 나아가려고 해요.
Now I'm going to forget the past and move forward.
과거 as 'bygones' one leaves behind
그 사람의 과거에 대해서는 잘 몰라요.
I don't really know about that person's past.
과거 = someone's personal history
nuance: 과거 is the past as an abstract span of time, and it contrasts directly with 현재 (present) and 미래 (future). It also refers to a person's personal history or 'past' and, in grammar, to the past tense (과거형). For a specific remembered time you would use 예전 or 옛날 in casual speech, while 과거 sounds slightly more formal and is common in writing.
mistakes: Don't use 과거 for 'last time / a while ago' in casual speech — use 예전 or 저번 there.
과거 is a noun, not a verb; to say 'in the past it was' use 과거에는 ~였어요, not 과거했어요.

usage: can stand alone as an adverb at the start of a sentence
현재까지의 결과 = the results so far
grammar term for the present-tense form
examples: 현재 서울에 살고 있어요.
I'm currently living in Seoul.
현재 used adverbially = 'at present'
현재까지 신청한 사람이 백 명이 넘어요.
So far, over a hundred people have applied.
현재까지 = up to now
과거나 미래보다 현재가 가장 중요해요.
The present matters more than the past or future.
현재 contrasted with 과거 and 미래
nuance: 현재 means 'the present' as a noun and also works as an adverb meaning 'currently / at present,' a bit more formal than 지금. In writing and news it often replaces 지금: 현재 상황, 현재까지. As a grammar term, 현재형 is the present tense. Use 지금 in everyday conversation and 현재 when the tone is more formal or written.
mistakes: 현재 is more formal than 지금; in casual chat 지금 sounds more natural.
Don't add 에 when using it as an adverb — say 현재 살고 있어요, not 현재에 살고 있어요.

usage: time adverbial for things to come
pairs with 밝은/어두운 to describe outlook
가까운/먼 미래 = the near / distant future
examples: 미래에는 자동차가 하늘을 날지도 몰라요.
In the future, cars might fly through the sky.
미래에(는) for predictions
아이들의 밝은 미래를 위해 열심히 일해요.
I work hard for the children's bright future.
밝은 미래 collocation
먼 미래보다 가까운 미래를 먼저 계획하세요.
Plan for the near future before the distant future.
가까운/먼 미래 contrast
nuance: 미래 is the future as an abstract concept and completes the set with 과거 and 현재. It pairs with adjectives like 밝은 (bright) or 어두운 (dark) and verbs like 준비하다 and 계획하다. For the more concrete '(this) coming time' such as next week you would use 앞으로 or 나중에 rather than 미래, which sounds broad and somewhat formal.
mistakes: Don't use 미래 to mean 'later today / soon' — use 나중에 or 이따가 for near, casual future.
'In the future I'll...' as a personal plan is more naturally 앞으로 ~할 거예요 than 미래에 ~.

usage: refers back to a specific instant just mentioned
보는 순간 = the instant one sees
adverb form describing a split-second reaction
pairs with 마지막/결정적인 for a crucial instant
examples: 그 순간 머릿속이 하얘졌어요.
At that moment my mind went blank.
그 순간 = at that very instant
문을 여는 순간 깜짝 놀랐어요.
The moment I opened the door, I was startled.
-는 순간 = the instant that
행복한 순간들은 늘 빨리 지나가요.
Happy moments always pass by quickly.
순간 as a countable 'moment'
nuance: 순간 is a single instant or fleeting moment, much shorter than 동안 (a stretch of time) or 시기 (a period). The pattern Verb-는 순간 means 'the moment/instant that something happens' and is extremely common for dramatic timing. 순간적으로 describes a reflexive, split-second action. Note it pairs with 지나가다 (pass by) for moments slipping away.
mistakes: Don't use 순간 for a duration like 'for a moment, please wait' — that's 잠깐/잠시, not 순간.
-는 순간 takes the present 는 even for past events: 문을 여는 순간 놀랐어요, not 연 순간.

usage: refers to a particular stretch of time or phase
시기 follows a noun naming the phase
pairs with 적절한/적당한 for opportune timing
놓치다 = to let the timing slip by
examples: 지금이 이사하기에 가장 좋은 시기예요.
Now is the best time to move.
시기 = an opportune period for doing something
취업을 준비하는 시기에는 스트레스가 많아요.
During the period of job hunting, there's a lot of stress.
-는 시기에(는) = during the phase of
좋은 시기를 놓치지 않으려고 서둘렀어요.
I hurried so as not to miss the good timing.
시기를 놓치다 collocation
nuance: 시기 is a period or phase of time defined by what is happening in it, broader than a 순간 but more specific than 시대 (an era). It often carries the sense of 'the right timing' for an action, as in 적절한 시기 or 시기를 놓치다. Compare 시기 (a phase, e.g., 성장 시기) with 기간 (a measured duration with a start and end, e.g., 시험 기간).
mistakes: Don't confuse 시기 (period/timing) with the homophone 시기 meaning 'envy/jealousy' — context disambiguates, but they are different words.
Use 기간 when you mean a measured duration (3-day period); 시기 is a phase or the right moment.

usage: at that time, in those days
the most common form, referring to a past time already in context
사고 당시 = at the time of the accident
examples: 그 당시에는 휴대폰이 없어서 많이 불편했어요.
Back then there were no cell phones, so it was very inconvenient.
그 당시에(는) = in those days
사고 당시 저는 집에 있었어요.
At the time of the accident, I was at home.
N 당시 = at the moment of that event
당시 저는 대학생이었어요.
At the time, I was a university student.
당시 placed before the clause it frames
nuance: 당시 means 'at that (past) time' and always points back to a specific time established in context, so it is most often used as 그 당시 or N 당시 (사고 당시, 졸업 당시). Unlike 그때, which is neutral and casual, 당시 sounds more formal and is common in narration, news, and written accounts. It cannot refer to the future or present.
mistakes: 당시 refers only to a past time; don't use it for 'now' or the future.
당시 is more formal than 그때; in casual conversation 그때 usually sounds more natural.

usage: the core adverbial form; almost always used with 에
expresses two things happening together or a dual quality
거의 softens to 'nearly at the same time'
examples: 두 사람이 동시에 같은 말을 했어요.
The two people said the same thing at the same time.
동시에 = simultaneously
그는 가수인 동시에 배우예요.
He is a singer and at the same time an actor.
N인 동시에 = is X and also Y
문을 닫는 동시에 비가 쏟아지기 시작했어요.
The moment I closed the door, rain started pouring at the same time.
-는 동시에 = simultaneously with the action
nuance: 동시 means 'the same time' and is nearly always used as 동시에 (simultaneously) or in the pattern -는/-인 동시에. With a verb it means two actions happen together; with a noun (N인 동시에) it means something has two qualities at once ('is X and also Y'). It differs from 한꺼번에, which stresses doing things 'all in one go' rather than precisely at the same instant.
mistakes: 동시 is rarely used bare — say 동시에, not just 동시, when you mean 'at the same time.'
Don't confuse 동시에 (simultaneously) with 한꺼번에 (all at once / in a single batch).

usage: often used adverbially without a particle
compound: a job one keeps for life
never forget for one's whole life
examples: 할머니는 평생 이 마을에서 사셨어요.
Grandmother lived in this village her whole life.
평생 used adverbially = 'all her life'
이 은혜는 평생 잊지 않을게요.
I'll never forget this kindness for the rest of my life.
평생 + negative for 'never in my life'
평생 한 번 있을까 말까 한 기회예요.
It's a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.
평생 emphasizing rarity across a whole life
nuance: 평생 means one's entire life span and is most often used adverbially ('for my whole life') without a particle, or as 평생 동안. It carries emotional weight, common in promises (평생 사랑할게요) and statements of rarity (평생 한 번). Compare 일생 (a lifetime, more bookish/biographical) — 평생 is the everyday word and feels heartfelt rather than clinical.
mistakes: 평생 already implies 'whole life,' so don't add 전체; 평생 동안 is the natural way to stress duration.
Don't write 평셍 or 평성 — the correct spelling is 평생.

usage: 순서대로 하다 = to do in the proper order
keep the order, wait one's turn
다음 순서는 누구예요? = whose turn is next?
examples: 번호 순서대로 들어가시면 됩니다.
You may go in in numerical order.
순서대로 = following the sequence
줄을 서서 순서를 지켜 주세요.
Please line up and wait your turn.
순서를 지키다 = observe the order
발표 순서가 갑자기 바뀌었어요.
The presentation order suddenly changed.
순서가 바뀌다 collocation
nuance: 순서 is the order or sequence in which things are arranged or done, and also a person's 'turn.' The set phrase 순서대로 ('in order') is essential, as is 순서를 지키다 ('wait your turn / keep the order'). It differs from 차례, a close synonym that leans toward 'one's turn' in a rotation; 순서 emphasizes the overall arrangement or sequence.
mistakes: Use 순서대로 (with 대로) for 'in order'; 순서로 alone sounds incomplete.
For 'it's my turn now,' 차례 is often more idiomatic: 이제 제 차례예요.

usage: 이 축제의 시초 = the origin of this festival
X이/가 시초가 되다 = X marks the beginning
a small misunderstanding was the start
examples: 이 작은 가게가 그 회사의 시초였어요.
This small shop was the beginning of that company.
N의 시초였다 = was the origin of N
사소한 말다툼이 큰 싸움의 시초가 됐어요.
A trivial argument became the start of a big fight.
시초가 되다 = to mark the beginning
그 발견이 현대 의학의 시초라고 해요.
That discovery is said to be the start of modern medicine.
시초 for a historical starting point
nuance: 시초 means the very beginning or origin of something, the point from which it all started. It is more formal and 'historical/origin' in flavor than the everyday 처음 (first time / at first) or 시작 (start of an activity). Use 시초 when tracing where something originated (a company, a custom, a conflict), often as N의 시초 or 시초가 되다.
mistakes: Don't use 시초 for 'at first / in the beginning' in casual speech — use 처음(에) for that.
시초 names the origin point; for starting an action use the verb 시작하다, not 시초하다 (not a word).

english: the final stage, the home stretch
usage: 막바지에 이르다 = to reach the final stage
이르다 = to arrive at a stage
summer is in its final days
N이/가 막바지다 = N is winding down
examples: 공사가 이제 막바지에 접어들었어요.
The construction has now entered its final stage.
막바지에 접어들다 = to enter the home stretch
시험 준비가 막바지라서 정말 바빠요.
Exam prep is in its final stretch, so I'm really busy.
N이/가 막바지다 = is in its last phase
올해도 어느덧 막바지에 이르렀네요.
This year has reached its final days before we knew it.
막바지에 이르다 collocation
nuance: 막바지 refers to the very last phase of something that has been going on for a while — a season, a project, a year — equivalent to 'the home stretch' or 'final stage.' It implies intensity or winding-down right before the end. Compare 막판, a more colloquial near-synonym, and 마지막, which simply means 'the last' without the 'final phase of a process' nuance.
mistakes: Don't use 막바지 for 'the last item/one' — that's 마지막; 막바지 is the final phase of an ongoing process.
Pair it with 이르다/접어들다/다다르다 for 'reach the home stretch,' not 가다.

english: in the meantime, during that time
usage: often used with 에; marks an interval between two points
change a lot in the meantime
그사이 무슨 일 있었어요? = did something happen in between?
emphasizes a short gap of time
examples: 잠깐 나갔다 왔는데 그사이에 비가 왔나 봐요.
I just stepped out and back, and it seems it rained in the meantime.
그사이에 = during that short interval
오랜만에 만났는데 그사이 아이가 많이 컸네요.
It's been a while since I saw them, and the child has grown a lot in the meantime.
그사이 stressing change over an interval
제가 자리를 비운 그사이에 무슨 일 있었어요?
Did something happen while I was away?
그사이에 = in the gap when one was absent
nuance: 그사이 (also written 그 사이) means 'in the meantime / during that interval,' referring to the gap between two moments — typically while someone was away or time quietly passed. It often appears as 그사이에 and frequently pairs with comments about unexpected change. Compare 그동안, which covers a longer ongoing stretch ('all this while'); 그사이 stresses a shorter in-between gap.
mistakes: 그사이 is commonly written as one word, but 그 사이 (spaced) is also accepted; keep it consistent.
Don't confuse 그사이 (a short interval) with 그동안 (the whole period up to now), which spans a longer time.

english: (the old) days, one's time/era of life
usage: the most common collocation, full of nostalgia
refers fondly to a remembered period
pairs with 좋은/힘든 to color the period
examples: 학창 시절이 가끔 너무 그리워요.
I sometimes miss my school days so much.
학창 시절 = one's school years
어린 시절에는 시골에서 자랐어요.
In my childhood, I grew up in the countryside.
어린 시절에(는) = during one's young days
그 시절에는 다들 가난했지만 행복했어요.
In those days everyone was poor but happy.
그 시절 evoking a nostalgic era
nuance: 시절 refers to a remembered period of one's life, almost always tinged with nostalgia, as in 학창 시절 (school days) or 어린 시절 (childhood). It is warmer and more personal than 시기 (a neutral phase) or 때 (a plain 'time when'). You would not use 시절 for the future — it looks back fondly on a bygone stage of life.
mistakes: Don't use 시절 for a future or neutral period; it is nostalgic and backward-looking.
시절 normally follows a descriptor (학창/어린/그) — using it bare to mean just 'time' sounds incomplete.
